title: Frailty: Measure Vulnerability, Then Match the Care Plan
bottomLine: Frailty is reduced physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors, not simply advanced age. Identify frailty and use a comprehensive geriatric approach to align medications, mobility, cognition, nutrition, function, social support and goals of care.
recognize: Weight loss, exhaustion, slowed gait, weakness, falls, functional decline and repeated hospitalizations can signal frailty.
differentiate: Frailty is distinct from disability and comorbidity, though they overlap.
assessment: Assess ADLs/IADLs, mobility, falls, cognition, mood, nutrition, continence, vision/hearing, medications, supports, caregiver strain and patient goals.
workup: Use a validated frailty scale and targeted testing for reversible contributors rather than broad age-based panels.
management: Use strength and mobility interventions, nutritional support, deprescribing, chronic-disease simplification and coordinated community services matched to goals and reserve.
medicationSafety: Standard disease targets can cause more harm in severe frailty if they increase hypotension, hypoglycemia or treatment burden.
counselling: Discuss what outcomes matter most—independence, symptom burden, longevity, staying home—before intensifying treatment.
followUp: Reassess function after acute illness because frailty can worsen and sometimes improve.
examTrap: Applying the same aggressive BP and glucose targets to a severely frail patient with recurrent falls and hypoglycemia without reconsidering goals.
oneLinePearl: Frailty changes the benefit-harm balance of almost every treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Frailty Network and Canadian geriatrics practice principles

title: Falls: Find the Contributors, Not Just the Bruise
bottomLine: A fall is often a syndrome produced by medications, orthostasis, gait or balance impairment, vision, footwear, environment, cognition and acute illness. Recurrent falls need multifactorial assessment rather than only imaging each injury.
recognize: Sedatives, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, neuropathy, vestibular disease and deconditioning are common contributors.
differentiate: Syncope, seizure and mechanical trip have different implications; ask what happened before the patient hit the ground.
assessment: Assess orthostatics when safe, gait/balance, feet/footwear, vision, medications, cognition, alcohol, home hazards, fracture risk and cardiac/neurologic symptoms.
workup: Use ECG, CBC, chemistry, imaging or vestibular/neuro testing only when the event history suggests them.
management: Use strength/balance exercise, medication review, vision/foot care, home modification, osteoporosis treatment and cause-specific intervention.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, anticholinergics and multiple BP-lowering agents commonly increase falls risk.
counselling: Avoid telling older adults simply to 'be more careful'; target modifiable risks without restricting activity unnecessarily.
followUp: Reassess after medication and mobility interventions.
examTrap: Prescribing a walker after recurrent falls without reviewing the patient's sedatives and orthostatic BP.
oneLinePearl: Falls prevention is a systems review of the person, not a single-device prescription.

title: Cognitive Decline: Dementia, Delirium, Depression, or Medication?
bottomLine: Dementia is persistent cognitive decline that interferes with function. Before labelling it irreversible, establish the trajectory, obtain collateral history and look for delirium, depression, medication effects, sensory impairment and selected reversible contributors.
recognize: Memory, executive function, language, visuospatial ability or behaviour may be affected depending on dementia subtype.
differentiate: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention; depression can mimic cognitive impairment; normal aging does not cause major functional loss.
assessment: Assess cognition and functional impact, driving, medications, sleep, mood, hearing/vision, vascular risk, neurologic signs and caregiver observations.
workup: Use a validated cognitive instrument plus targeted CBC, B12, TSH and other testing based on phenotype; neuroimaging is indicated when atypical, focal, rapid or otherwise clinically warranted, not universally.
management: Treat vascular and sensory contributors, use cognitive-enhancing medication for appropriate diagnoses, support function and safety and provide caregiver resources.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics and sedatives can worsen cognition; cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia, GI effects and syncope.
counselling: Discuss diagnosis directly with the capable patient and include chosen supports with consent.
followUp: Reassess cognition, function, driving, caregiver strain and advance-care planning longitudinally.
examTrap: Diagnosing dementia during an acute fluctuating hospitalization without establishing the pre-illness cognitive baseline.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is chronic decline in cognition plus function; delirium is acute brain failure.
sourceBasis: Canadian geriatrics and dementia practice resources

title: Driving and Cognition: Functional Risk, Not Age Alone
bottomLine: Driving fitness is determined by functional abilities and medical risk, not chronological age or diagnosis alone. Cognitive impairment, syncope, seizure, vision loss and medication effects may require formal assessment or reporting under provincial law.
recognize: Getting lost, near-misses, new crashes, caregiver concern and impaired executive or visuospatial function are important clues.
differentiate: A dementia diagnosis does not automatically determine driving fitness at every stage; a normal office cognitive screen does not prove safe driving.
assessment: Ask crashes, citations, getting lost, driving avoidance, visual and motor function, cognition, medication sedation and family observations.
workup: Use jurisdiction-approved medical and functional driving assessment pathways; road testing may be required when office assessment is inconclusive.
management: Treat reversible contributors, counsel driving restriction when risk is unacceptable and fulfill mandatory or discretionary reporting obligations according to province or territory.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, opioids, first-generation antihistamines and hypoglycemia-producing drugs can impair driving even without dementia.
redFlags: Seizure not meeting jurisdictional control interval
counselling: Discuss transportation alternatives and preserve autonomy where possible rather than framing driving cessation as punishment.
followUp: Document counselling, reports and reassessment plan.
examTrap: Telling every person over 80 to stop driving solely because of age.
oneLinePearl: Driving is a functional competency, not an age-based privilege test.

title: Polypharmacy: Deprescribe With an Indication and a Taper Plan
bottomLine: Polypharmacy risk comes from medication burden, interactions and mismatch with goals—not from an arbitrary pill count. For every drug, identify indication, benefit, harm, duration and what happens if it is reduced or stopped.
recognize: Falls, orthostasis, confusion, constipation, urinary retention, bleeding and hypoglycemia are common medication-related geriatric syndromes.
differentiate: Appropriate multidrug treatment can be beneficial; the goal is not minimum medications but maximum net benefit.
assessment: Reconcile prescriptions, OTCs, supplements, duplicate prescribers, adherence, renal/hepatic function and patient priorities.
workup: Use drug-specific labs and symptom review; avoid adding another drug to treat an unrecognized adverse effect when deprescribing can solve the problem.
management: Prioritize stopping high-harm low-benefit therapy, taper withdrawal-prone drugs and simplify regimens; coordinate prescribers and pharmacy.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines, beta blockers, clonidine, corticosteroids, antidepressants and some antiseizure drugs may require tapering rather than abrupt cessation.
counselling: Frame deprescribing as active treatment optimization, not abandonment.
followUp: Monitor withdrawal, symptom recurrence and function after each meaningful change.
examTrap: Stopping five long-term medications at once in a frail patient and then being unable to identify which change caused deterioration.
oneLinePearl: Deprescribe deliberately enough to learn from the change.

title: Malnutrition and Sarcopenia: Weight Alone Misses Risk
bottomLine: Older adults can be malnourished at any body size. Unintentional weight loss, low intake, loss of muscle strength or function and acute illness should trigger nutrition and sarcopenia assessment.
recognize: Chewing/swallowing problems, depression, dementia, medications, isolation, poverty and chronic inflammation can reduce intake or muscle mass.
differentiate: Obesity does not exclude sarcopenia or micronutrient deficiency.
assessment: Assess weight trajectory, intake, dentition, swallowing, hand grip/function, food access, GI symptoms, mood and social isolation.
workup: Use targeted CBC, chemistry, thyroid, inflammatory or malabsorption tests based on the clinical picture; dietitian assessment often adds more value than broad labs.
management: Treat causes, increase protein and energy intake when appropriate, add resistance exercise and connect to meal or income supports.
medicationSafety: Appetite stimulants can cause thrombotic, delirium or other harms and are not routine first-line care.
counselling: Discuss nutrition without assuming weight loss is desirable because the patient is overweight.
followUp: Track intake, strength, weight and function.
examTrap: Congratulating an older adult with obesity on a 12-kg unintentional weight loss without assessing malnutrition or cancer.
oneLinePearl: Unintentional weight loss is a symptom, not a success metric.

title: Pressure Injury: Offload the Cause, Do Not Just Dress the Wound
bottomLine: Pressure injury treatment requires pressure redistribution, moisture control, nutrition and mobility support in addition to wound care. Deep tissue injury can be worse than the skin surface initially suggests.
recognize: Risk rises with immobility, neuropathy, incontinence, poor perfusion, malnutrition and medical devices.
differentiate: Moisture-associated dermatitis is diffuse and superficial; arterial ulcers and diabetic foot ulcers have different perfusion/neuropathy drivers.
assessment: Stage the injury correctly, assess undermining, infection, pain, perfusion, nutrition, continence, equipment and ability to reposition.
workup: Do not culture chronic wounds routinely without clinical infection; evaluate osteomyelitis when deep tissue or bone involvement is plausible.
management: Offload/reposition, use pressure-relieving surfaces, optimize nutrition and moisture, debride appropriately and treat infection when present.
medicationSafety: Topical or systemic antibiotics are not routine for colonized noninfected pressure injuries.
counselling: Include caregivers in realistic turning and equipment plans without blaming them for injury.
followUp: Track wound dimensions and healing trajectory and reassess pressure sources.
examTrap: Ordering antibiotics because a chronic pressure wound has a positive surface swab but no clinical infection.
oneLinePearl: Pressure wounds heal when pressure changes.

title: Mistreatment of Older Persons: Capacity Does Not Cancel Safety Assessment
bottomLine: Mistreatment can be physical, psychological, financial, sexual or neglect and often occurs in relationships of trust. Speak with the older person privately when safe, assess immediate danger and capacity, respect autonomous choices, and follow local legal duties without assuming age or dependence means incapacity.
recognize: Unexplained injuries, fear, isolation, missing money, controlling companions, poor access to medications or food and caregiver conflict can be warning signs.
differentiate: Self-neglect, caregiver strain and intentional abuse can overlap but require different responses; a warning sign does not prove abuse.
assessment: Ask privately whether the person feels safe, who controls money/medications, whether anyone threatens or restricts them, and assess cognition/capacity and immediate danger.
workup: Document objective findings and obtain injury or financial/social assessment as appropriate; legal reporting duties differ across provinces/territories and care settings.
management: Treat injuries, create a patient-led safety plan when the person is capable, involve social work/community resources and emergency services for imminent danger; follow mandatory reporting law where applicable.
medicationSafety: Medication withholding, over-sedation and unauthorized administration can themselves be forms of mistreatment.
redFlags: Financial exploitation with loss of essentials
counselling: Do not confront the suspected abusive person in a way that increases risk after the patient leaves.
followUp: Keep access to care open even when a capable person declines a proposed intervention.
examTrap: Assuming an older adult with intact capacity must accept removal from home because the clinician thinks it is safer.
oneLinePearl: Safety planning must protect autonomy as well as safety when capacity is intact.
sourceBasis: PHAC mistreatment of older persons resources
provincial and territorial adult protection law

title: Advance Care Planning: Values Before Crisis Orders
bottomLine: Advance care planning explores values, acceptable outcomes and substitute decision arrangements before crisis. It is not the same as a current medical order for CPR or treatment limitations, which must be based on the present clinical context and local law.
recognize: Serious illness, frailty, progressive neurologic disease and repeated hospitalization are opportunities for anticipatory discussions.
differentiate: Advance directive, goals-of-care discussion, substitute decision-maker appointment and current resuscitation order are related but distinct legal/clinical concepts.
assessment: Assess capacity, illness understanding, values, prior conversations, substitute decision arrangements and what tradeoffs matter to the person.
workup: No test determines goals; prognosis estimates should be communicated with uncertainty.
management: Document values and decision-makers clearly and translate them into current treatment recommendations when decisions arise.
medicationSafety: A comfort-focused plan still requires active medication review and safe symptom treatment.
counselling: Use plain language about CPR, ventilation and hospital treatment rather than vague 'do everything' terminology.
followUp: Revisit plans when health status or goals change.
examTrap: Treating an advance-care-planning conversation as if it were automatically a valid do-not-resuscitate order in every future circumstance.
oneLinePearl: Values guide decisions; clinical orders implement them in a specific context.
sourceBasis: Canadian Hospice Palliative Care and provincial advance-care planning resources

title: Palliative Symptom Crisis: Relieve Suffering While Reversible Causes Stay Proportionate
bottomLine: Dyspnea, pain, nausea, agitation and secretions at end of life require rapid symptom relief guided by goals and proportionality. A comfort-focused plan does not mean ignoring reversible causes when treating them aligns with the person's goals.
recognize: Terminal delirium, dyspnea and escalating opioid needs can occur in the final days, but urinary retention, constipation, infection or medication toxicity may still be reversible contributors.
differentiate: Palliative sedation for refractory suffering is a distinct practice from routine symptom medication and from MAID.
assessment: Assess symptom severity, likely reversible contributors, goals, swallowing route, renal/hepatic function, caregiver capacity and current medications.
workup: Limit tests to those likely to change a goal-concordant treatment plan.
management: Use opioid, antiemetic, anxiolytic or antipsychotic strategies appropriate to the symptom and organ function; use non-drug comfort measures and specialist palliative consultation for refractory suffering.
medicationSafety: Opioids titrated proportionally for dyspnea or pain are ethically and clinically distinct from intentionally causing death; renal failure changes opioid selection and metabolite risk.
redFlags: Caregiver unable to safely administer home medications
counselling: Prepare family for expected changes and provide explicit crisis medication instructions.
followUp: Ensure after-hours access and medication supply match the care setting.
examTrap: Withholding appropriately titrated opioid for severe end-of-life dyspnea because of fear that any respiratory slowing means euthanasia.
oneLinePearl: Palliative medication is titrated to relieve suffering proportionately.

title: MAID in Canada: Eligibility, Voluntariness, Capacity, and Safeguards
bottomLine: Canadian law permits eligible physicians and nurse practitioners to assess and provide MAID when federal eligibility criteria and procedural safeguards are met, along with provincial or territorial standards. MAID is patient-requested care: family preference cannot initiate or authorize it for an incapable person.
recognize: Federal criteria include adulthood, decision-making capacity, a voluntary request free of external pressure, informed consent and a grievous and irremediable medical condition as defined in law.
differentiate: MAID, palliative sedation, withdrawal of burdensome treatment and suicide prevention are legally and clinically distinct practices.
As of August 2026, eligibility where mental illness is the sole underlying condition remains delayed until March 17, 2027.
assessment: Assess capacity for the MAID decision, voluntariness, coercion, suffering, available means to relieve suffering and whether the request fits federal and local criteria; use trauma-informed and culturally safe practice.
workup: Two independent practitioner assessments and required documentation/safeguards apply; additional safeguards differ depending on whether natural death is reasonably foreseeable.
management: Follow the Criminal Code, Health Canada model standard and the applicable provincial or territorial regulator/program; clinicians unwilling or unable to participate must follow their jurisdiction's professional obligations while continuing unrelated care.
medicationSafety: MAID medications, prescribing, storage, pharmacy communication and reporting follow specialized legal/professional protocols and are not routine prescribing.
redFlags: Request initiated by someone other than the patient
counselling: Present palliative, disability, psychosocial and community supports without coercing acceptance or framing disability as lower quality of life.
followUp: Maintain confidentiality, required reporting and continuity of non-MAID care.
examTrap: Accepting a family member's request for MAID on behalf of an incapable adult who never made the qualifying patient request.
oneLinePearl: MAID requires the patient's voluntary legally qualifying request—not substitute consent.
sourceBasis: Health Canada Model Practice Standard for MAID
